name: Hairline stack (fin + min + derma roll)

card.summary: A combined routine of finasteride, minoxidil and microneedling (derma rolling) used to hold or thicken the hairline and scalp hair.
card.note: Finasteride is prescription-only and has reported sexual and mood side effects; see a clinician.

quick.overview:
The hairline stack combines three treatments for male pattern hair loss: oral finasteride, which lowers DHT; topical minoxidil, which stimulates growth; and derma rolling, a form of microneedling of the scalp. People use it to keep or thicken the hair frame around the face.

Research exists on the individual parts and on some pairings. A 2025 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials found adding microneedling to minoxidil improved hair count versus minoxidil alone, though results varied widely between trials.
quick.how: The three components are used in parallel: a daily oral prescription medication, a topical solution or foam on the scalp, and periodic microneedling sessions. Forums often describe it as a baseline regimen and discuss adding other items such as ketoconazole shampoo. Hair change takes months, and benefits last only while treatment continues.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists gynecomastia, erectile dysfunction and depression as reported finasteride side effects, and increased shedding has been reported with minoxidil. In the microneedling meta-analysis, adverse events were more frequent with the combination (74 vs 59 events) but typically mild. Finasteride requires a prescription and medical guidance.

lead: The hairline stack is a community term for combining finasteride, minoxidil and derma rolling to treat androgenetic hair loss. It targets thinning at the hairline and temples, which strongly affects how the face frames.

Each part has a distinct role. Hair loss is linked to dihydrotestosterone formed by 5-alpha-reductase in hair follicles, and finasteride addresses that pathway; minoxidil is applied topically and is the only topical product FDA-approved for androgenic alopecia, per Wikipedia; microneedling adds mechanical stimulation of the scalp.[1]

Wikipedia reports that combining finasteride, minoxidil and ketoconazole is more effective than any one alone, and that pairing finasteride or minoxidil with microneedling or low-level laser showed substantive increases in hair count.[1] A 2025 meta-analysis of randomized trials supports microneedling plus minoxidil over minoxidil alone.[2]

chain: Finasteride reduces DHT's effect on follicles
Minoxidil stimulates growth and Microneedling stimulates the scalp
Hair loss slows and density can increase
angle.text: The stack uses three mechanisms at once to hold the hairline and add density. Users commonly report it as a baseline retention routine.

paras: Finasteride: Wikipedia reports about a 30% improvement after six months in men, with benefit lasting only while the drug is taken, and lists gynecomastia, erectile dysfunction and depression among side effects.[1]
Minoxidil: about 40% of men regrow hair in three to six months according to Wikipedia, and increased hair loss has been reported.[1]
Microneedling: use of a derma roller or pen to create small scalp punctures; evidence is mostly in combination with minoxidil.[2]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Archives of Dermatological Research pooled 10 randomized trials (587 participants) and found combined microneedling plus minoxidil improved hair count versus minoxidil alone (standardised mean difference 1.32), with high heterogeneity. Hair diameter also improved, and microneedling depth, duration and device type did not significantly change results.[2]
Adverse events were more frequent with the combination (74 vs 59) but mostly mild or self-limiting.[2]
Studies of the specific three-way stack were not found. Trials cited above examine microneedling with minoxidil and reviews describe finasteride and minoxidil together.[1][2]
